name: Stakeholder Analysis
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Whose Trust Are You Actually Building? Stakeholder Analysis for Blockchain Systems
lesson.summary: Stakeholder analysis identifies everyone with a real interest in a system's success, not just the customer paying for it, and surfaces the conflicting requirements a blockchain architecture has to reconcile before anyone writes a line of code.
lesson.body:
A blockchain project usually has a client or a founder who defines the vision, but that person is almost never the only party whose interests the architecture has to serve. Stakeholder analysis is the practice of systematically identifying every group with a real stake in a system, understanding what each one needs, and recognizing where those needs conflict, before architecture decisions lock those conflicts in permanently.

The connection to architecture is immediate once the list of stakeholders is written out. Node operators want low hardware and bandwidth requirements, because they bear the ongoing computational cost covered earlier in this chapter. Miners or validators want meaningful fee revenue and predictable rewards, because their capital and equipment are on the line. End users want low fees and fast confirmation. Regulators, when a project touches real money, want auditability and the ability to trace illicit activity. Application developers want stable, well documented interfaces that will not break with every protocol upgrade. A single architecture cannot fully satisfy all of these groups at once, and pretending otherwise just pushes the conflict downstream to whichever stakeholder has the least power to complain when the tradeoff finally shows up.

This is also where stakeholder analysis exposes the limits of business requirements taken at face value. A written business requirement usually reflects the view of whoever commissioned the project, typically a founder or an executive sponsor, and that view rarely captures needs that no one in the room happens to hold. A compliance officer's requirement that transactions be traceable for anti money laundering purposes can sit in direct tension with a privacy focused user base that chose the platform specifically to avoid that kind of surveillance. Neither party is wrong, but only a deliberate stakeholder analysis, one that goes out and asks rather than assuming the founder's list is complete, will surface that tension before the architecture is built around one side's assumptions.

Bitcoin's own history offers a real and well documented example of what happens when stakeholder conflict plays out in public. The block size debate that ran roughly from 2015 through 2017 pitted a rough coalition favoring larger blocks, which would lower transaction fees and please everyday users and some businesses, against developers and node operators worried that larger blocks would raise the hardware cost of running a full node, pushing verification toward fewer, more centralized parties. That disagreement never fully reconciled through discussion alone, and it ultimately produced a split, with Bitcoin Cash forking away in 2017 as one faction's answer to a stakeholder conflict the existing architecture could not satisfy for everyone simultaneously.

Stakeholder analysis matters practically because it determines who gets a voice when a utility tree assigns those high, medium, or low importance ratings to competing scenarios. A utility tree built by engineers alone, without a genuine stakeholder analysis feeding into it, tends to rate technical elegance highly and regulatory or user experience concerns as afterthoughts, producing an architecture that is well engineered and poorly adopted. Doing the stakeholder work first is what keeps the prioritization exercise honest.
